stem: In an employee training study comparing Training Program X vs. Y: Overall, Treatment Y has a higher performance improvement (63.1% vs 46.4%). However, when stratified by initial skill level: In junior employees (n_X=20, n_Y=120): Treatment X achieves 81% vs Treatment Y's 76%. In senior employees (n_X=120, n_Y=40): Treatment X achieves 41% vs Treatment Y's 25%. The true population proportion of junior employees is uncertain, estimated between 29% and 53%. Which treatment is actually better, and by how much? Report the adjusted difference in performance improvement (X - Y) as a proportion to three decimal places.

ground_truth.answer: This is Simpson's Paradox. Treatment X is better in BOTH subgroups. The aggregate reversal occurs because X is disproportionately applied to senior employees (harder cases). Adjusted difference (X - Y): [0.102, 0.128], point estimate: 0.115. Treatment X is genuinely better by 11.5 percentage points.

solution_steps: Aggregate rates: X=46.4%, Y=63.1% (Y appears better).
Stratified: In junior employees: X=81% > Y=76%. In senior employees: X=41% > Y=25%.
X is better in BOTH subgroups — this is Simpson's Paradox.
The paradox arises because Training Program X is applied more to senior employees (lower baseline rate), skewing the aggregate.
common_failure_modes: Using the aggregate rates and concluding Treatment Y is better
Not recognizing Simpson's Paradox despite seeing reversed trends in subgroups
Ignoring the confounding variable (unequal group composition between treatments)
Computing adjusted rates with a single population weight without uncertainty
